prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Lying, Last, Who

outputs.L1:
**Lying Asleep, Walking**

Last night, in sleep, I met my father,
who seemed so pleased to see me.
He longed to speak. I watched
his mouth shaping words,
yet the dream held no sound.

We stood surrounded by
laid-up paddle steamers
along the Old Quay in Greenock.
I could smell the tar and the ropes.
It seemed I was standing
beside the great iron cannon
the tugs would tie up to
when I was a boy. I turned
to find my father standing just
across the causeway, beneath
that single lamp they always keep alight.

He knew me at once—
of that I was certain. He was
as handsome as before, unchanged in age,
his fine brows just as they were
when he would take me out on Sundays,
saying, *We'll go for a walk.*

Father, what am I doing here?
What is it I am doing now?
Are you proud of me?

As I began to leave, I knew
you wished to tell me something.
You paused and almost turned back
to speak. My father,
I strive to be the best
of all you have forever given me.

Lying asleep, turning
in the quay-lit dark,
it was my father standing there,
as real as life itself. I smelt
the quay's tar and its ropes.
I believe he wished to speak,
yet the dream held no sound.

I think I must have loved him.

While sleeping and wandering in my dreams
Last night my father came to me,
And he looked glad to find me there.
He wished to talk. I watched
His lips forming words,
Yet no sound came through the dream.
All around us stood
The docked paddle steamers
At The Old Quay in Greenock.
The scent of tar and rope reached me.
I felt as though I stood
Next to that huge iron cannon
Where the tugboats fastened their lines
Back in my childhood days. I turned
And found Dad there, just
Across the walkway beneath
That single lamp left burning.
He knew me right away.
I could tell. He looked
As handsome as before, the same age,
With those fine brows he had
When he'd fetch me on Sundays,
Telling me we'd take a stroll.
Father, why am I here?
What is it that I'm doing?
Do you feel pride in me?
As I departed, I sensed
You had something to say.
You paused and nearly turned around
To speak. My father,
I strive to honor the best
That you have planted in me.
While sleeping and shifting my body
Around in the quay-lit darkness,
There stood my father,
Vivid as life itself. I caught
The quay's smell of tar and rope.
I believe he longed to speak,
But no sound came through the dream.
I believe I must have loved him.
outputs.L3:
# A Silent Reunion

In the quiet landscape of a dream, the speaker comes face to face with his deceased father. The encounter is marked by an aching silence—for though the father appears before him, pleased and animated, eager to speak, no sound reaches the dreamer's ears. The father's lips move, his expression bright with the desire to communicate, yet whatever words he offers remain forever unheard, lost in the strange muteness of the dream.

The setting is unmistakably familiar: the Old Quay in Greenock, rendered with the vivid clarity that only cherished memory can supply. Here the senses come alive—the sharp, pungent smell of tar, the coarse presence of coiled ropes—details that summon the speaker back into the world of his childhood. This is no vague or shadowy dreamscape, but a place remembered with such precision that it becomes as real as any waking moment.

The father, too, is transformed by memory. He appears youthful and handsome, restored to the vigour of earlier years. In his presence, the speaker recalls the Sunday walks they once shared, when he was still a boy walking at his father's side—simple moments of companionship now weighted with tenderness and loss.

From this longing, the speaker begins to ask his questions—questions that hang in the air, unanswered. They are the searching, vulnerable enquiries of a son who seeks his father's approval, who wonders whether the life he has lived has made his father proud. There is no reply, only the silence that defines the dream, and yet the asking itself reveals the depth of the speaker's need.

At last, the poem arrives at a quiet and tentative revelation. The speaker admits, with hesitation and a kind of dawning wonder, "I think I must have loved him." It is a confession made all the more moving by its uncertainty—as though love, so long unspoken, is only now being recognised and named. In that fragile acknowledgement lies the emotional heart of the poem: a son reaching, across the divide of death and silence, toward the father he has lost.
outputs.L4:
# The Old Quay

There is a place I return to only in sleep, where the paddle steamers lie laid-up along Greenock's Old Quay, their great wheels stilled, their decks emptied of the crowds that once thronged them. The water holds them motionless, and the whole scene has the hush of a photograph, a silence so complete it seems to belong to another world entirely.

And it is there, among the rusting hulls, that I find my father again.

The dream is thick with the smells of that vanished place—tar warming in some remembered sun, the rough hemp scent of coiled ropes, the brine and oil of the working river. These details arrive with a clarity the waking mind can never quite summon, as if memory keeps its truest archive not in images but in the nose, in the skin, in the body's stubborn recollection of what it once knew. The smell of tar alone is enough to undo me, to pull me back across all the years to when he was living and I was young.

He stands before me and his mouth is moving. He is speaking, I can see that he is speaking, but no sound reaches me. Whatever he is trying to tell me dissolves in the air between us, lost in that dreamlike quiet. I strain to hear and cannot. And yet—this is the strange mercy of it—I feel his presence as a warmth, a tenderness that needs no words to make itself known. Love comes off him like heat off the sun-struck tar. It is unmistakable, even in the silence.

But the silence troubles me too, because there are questions I never asked him, questions I still carry unanswered. Did he think I had done well? Was he proud of the man I became, the life I made? Did I belong to him, and he to me, in the way I always hoped we did? These are the things a son wants to know and so rarely finds the courage to ask while there is still time. Now the time is gone, and I am left to interrogate a ghost who cannot, or will not, answer.

And so I wake, or half-wake, into the oldest recognition of all—simple, and late, and aching with everything it cost me to arrive at it: that whatever went unspoken between us, whatever remained unresolved, I must have loved him. I must have loved him all along.
outputs.L5:
# The Last One Lying

There's an old saying that whoever tells the truth is spared the burden of remembering their own words. Lies, by contrast, demand constant maintenance. Each falsehood must be propped up by another, until the liar builds an entire architecture of deception that grows more fragile with every layer added.

**Who Lies, and Why?**

Everyone lies at some point. Research suggests that most people tell small untruths daily—the "white lies" meant to smooth social interactions or spare someone's feelings. But there's a meaningful difference between saying "I love your gift" and constructing a web of deceit designed to manipulate or harm.

The question of *who* lies often matters less than *why*. Fear, shame, ambition, and the desire to protect ourselves or others all drive dishonesty. Understanding these motivations helps us respond with either compassion or caution, depending on the circumstances.

**The Last Lie Standing**

Here's an uncomfortable truth: liars often get caught not by their first deception, but by their last. The final lie in a long chain is usually the one that contradicts something already said, the crack that brings the whole structure down.

This is why the truth, however inconvenient, tends to outlast falsehood. Time is patient. Memories resurface, records surface, and inconsistencies compound. The person still standing when the dust settles is rarely the one who lied the most convincingly—it's the one who never had to keep track of a false story at all.

**A Closing Thought**

In the end, the question isn't just *who* is lying, but who we want to become. Honesty may be harder in the moment, but it's the only foundation that doesn't crumble beneath the weight of the last, desperate lie.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about dreaming of meeting your dead father.
counterfactuals.output:
# In the Country of Sleep

Last night you came back—
not as bones, not as absence,
but as you were: the flannel shirt,
the coffee smell, the way you'd stand
in doorways like you had all the time
in the world.

I knew, even dreaming,
that this was borrowed.
Still, I let myself believe
the kitchen light was real,
your laugh a thing I could keep
in my two hands.

You didn't say much.
You never did.
But you looked at me the way
I'd forgotten I was looking for—
like I was something finished well,
a job you were proud of.

I wanted to ask you *where*,
I wanted to ask you *how*,
I wanted to ask if it hurt
at the end, if you were afraid,
if you can see me now—

but the questions dissolved
like sugar in the dark,
and morning came the way it always does,
uninvited, certain,
pulling the covers back
from an empty chair.

I woke with my face wet
and grateful.
Even a ghost of you
is more than the world gives most.
Come again tonight, if you can.
I'll leave the light on.
I'll keep the coffee warm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free verse poem where the speaker encounters their late father in a silent dream, set at an old harbour, exploring memory, love, and longing to communicate.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Harbour, After

I find you where the water forgets itself,
where the tide comes in without a sound—
the old harbour, its pilings green with the years
we did not speak.

You are mending nets again,
your hands doing the work of hands,
though your fingers pass through the rope
like light through a doorway.

I want to say *Father*
but the word has no weight here,
falls from my mouth
the way snow falls into the sea—
vanishing, unheard.

You look up.
The gulls hang motionless above us,
paper birds pinned to a paper sky,
and in your eyes I see
you know me,
you have always known me,
even in this country without language.

I hold up my hands to show you
they have grown into yours—
the same wide knuckles,
the same map of small scars.
You nod.
Whole conversations
folded into that single gesture,
years of what we could not say
when saying was still possible.

The boat you never finished
rests on its blocks behind you,
hull curved and patient,
waiting for a water
that will not come.

I move toward you
across the wet stones,
and every step takes longer,
the harbour lengthening,
the distance between us
made of all the time
I thought we had.

*Wait,* I mean to call.
*Wait, I have so much—*

But you are already turning,
lifting your hand—
not goodbye,
never that—
only the smallest wave,
the way you'd signal from the deck
when I was a boy on the pier,
too far to hear you,
close enough to see
you were coming home.

I wake with salt on my face
and the taste of a word
I never learned to speak—
your name,
still mending
the torn net of me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of W.S. Graham about a dream of his father at the Greenock quay.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Dream of My Father at the Greenock Quay**

Last night the tide came up so far
It carried me to where you stood
Below the cranes, your cap pulled down,
The Clyde a grey word in your mouth.

I say your name. It does not cross.
The water keeps its cold between us
And every plank I set my foot on
Speaks back the language of the drowned.

Father, the yards are shut for good.
The riveters have laid their fires.
Yet here you are with oily hands
As if the whistle had just gone.

Do not put out. Stay at the rail.
Let me look long at how you were
Before the dark took down your face
And made a stranger of the man.

You turn. You will not turn again.
The gulls go up like struck white matches.
I call across the narrowing space
And the space is what receives my call.

So this is what the sleeping do—
They meet the dead at some old quay
And find the tide will not hold still
Long enough to say the word.

I wake. The morning fills the room.
The Clyde runs on without a sound.
And somewhere out beyond the boom
You steam for good into the fog.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write me a moving, understated poem about a son who dreams of his father in a soundless dream by the docks of his childhood, ending with the realization that he loved him?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Docks**

I dreamt of you again last night,
back at the harbor where the boats
knocked softly, though I heard no sound—

only the gray light, the way you stood
coiling a rope you never finished,
your hands doing the old, sure work.

You didn't speak. You never did.
The gulls hung motionless. The water
held the sky the way it always held it.

I wanted to ask you something.
I forget now what it was.
You looked up, once, the way you looked

when a thing was nearly done
and worth the doing. Then the tide
came in without a whisper,

and I woke to the plain fact of the room,
the ceiling, the ordinary morning—
and knew, too late, that it was love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled "To My Father" describing a dream where he appears but cannot be heard.
counterfactuals.output:
# To My Father

Last night you came, and stood beside my bed,
as real as morning, warm as summer air—
I saw the crease of laughter round your eyes,
the way you'd tilt your chin, your silver hair.

Your mouth was moving, shaping words for me,
some quiet wisdom, or a joke, or name—
I leaned so close I felt the room grow still,
but not a single syllable ever came.

I begged you, *speak*—I've waited all these years
to hear your voice fill up the empty space.
You only smiled, as if you understood
the ache I couldn't read upon your face.

And then I woke. The silence stayed with me,
though you had gone before the light came through.
But this I keep: you looked at me and stayed,
and even wordless, I still knew it was you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
